Download the packet as a PDF (27 Letter pages). Print it at actual size (100%), on both sides: each character, the reference, the map and the counters then have a sheet of their own.

Grave Wounds

The escalade: one fight on the rampart of Badajoz, and the week after

Version 0.1, 25 November 2026, for 3 to 5 people and about 3 hours. One person is the GM.

What this is. Grave Wounds is a d100 game built on real wound records. Where a man is hit comes from the graves and surgeons' returns of his own war. A fight usually ends with men stopping, not dying, and what happens afterwards can kill them just as well. This module sets four men of a British company of foot at the foot of a ladder against the bastion of San Vicente at Badajoz, on the night of 6 April 1812, while the storm of the breaches fails on the far side of the town. Their fight is to get up the ladder and hold the rampart. Then the town is sacked, and the week after it is theirs to get through.

What we want to learn. Are the fights tense and quick enough? Do the ladders and the reloading make the fight different from a medieval one? Do wounds feel fair? Nobody has played this at a table yet, so a blunt "this dragged" is the most useful thing you can tell us.

What you need. Pencils, two ten-sided dice for d100, scissors, and these pages. Everything to play on paper is here, with a hex map of the rampart and counters to cut out at the back. If you'd rather, a phone or laptop can run the fight: the wound roller does the arithmetic. Open swares.github.io/grave-wounds/dist/team.html#escalade. It sets up the four men against the French on this map, with the ladders, the night and the fires, and the GM's script can play the French. Please tell us which way you played.

The fight

A round is 6 seconds. Every fighter gets one turn, highest initiative first. Each man rolls once at the start: d10 + Agility ÷ 10, rounded down.

The one roll. Roll d100. Equal to or under the number succeeds, and how far under is the margin. A roll at or under a tenth of the number is a critical.

On his turn

  1. Move. Stay, advance up to 4 hexes and still attack, or run up to 12 and not attack. Walking away from an enemy beside you gives him a free attack.
  2. Attack. d100 against Attack, less your penalties. You may first declare an aim at a zone, at a gap in the armour, or both. Each costs 20 of your margin on a hit, and is free on a critical.
  3. Defence. The defender rolls d100 against Defence, less his penalties. Success turns the blow. A critical can't be defended.
  4. Where it lands. d100 on Where it lands, under the attacker's weapon. With the bayonet or a sabre, the attacker chooses cut or thrust before he rolls. A ball from a musket or pistol is a shot. A musket or pistol that has fired is empty: a musket shoots every third round, a pistol every fifth, and meanwhile its man fights with the bayonet, or the pistol's butt.
  5. How bad. Margin under 20: light. 20 or more: serious. 50 or more, or a critical: critical. A margin of 2 or less only grazes, unless it is a critical: a step less bleeding and pain, and no stop check.
  6. Armour. Armour lowers the severity by steps. See Where it lands.
  7. The wound. Read it from What it does and write it on the sheet.
  8. Stop check. A serious or critical wound marked S needs d100 against the wounded man's Nerve, less his pain and blood penalties, and 10 more for a critical. Players' men add their setting's bonus.
Result He is Which means
Equal or under Fighting on No change
Failed by 1–20 Defend only for 2 rounds No attack; he may move and defend
Failed by 21–40 Stunned for 2 rounds No attack; −50% to his defence
Failed by more than 40 Out of the fight until helped or the fight ends Takes no part: no attack, no defence

End of the round. Everyone bleeds. Then a side with 25% or more of its men down, or whose leader went down this round, rolls d100 against the best Nerve among those still up: +10 while a leader is up, −20 if he is down, −20 once 50% of the side is down. Over the target, the side breaks: it runs or surrenders.

Lethality. Standard: Blood ×1.5, +20 to Nerve on stop checks, and one fate point, which lowers a wound a step, or rerolls a stop check, recovery or fever roll. Gritty: Blood ×1, no bonus, no fate.

A worked shot

Donald shoots at 42% and rolls 20: a margin of 22, serious. The fusilier dodges at 35% and rolls 72, so it hits. On the musket column, a 28 is the right chest. He wears no armour, so it stays serious. The shot table gives B3 P2 S and hours: bleeding step B3, which the Bleeding table makes 3 Blood a round; pain step P2; a stop check, Nerve 50, less 20 for pain; and, left untreated, it kills in hours. Donald's musket is now empty: he shoots again in the third round.

Wounds

A wound has five parts, and they add up across all of a man's wounds. Bleed (B) and pain (P) are steps, not points: B2 is the second bleeding step, and the Bleeding table below gives the Blood it costs.

Bleeding. Every man has a Blood pool, on his sheet.

Bleed Blood lost What it is
B0 none None
B1 1 a minute Slow: seeping; lose 1 Blood per minute
B2 1 a round Heavy: lose 1 Blood per round; bind within minutes
B3 3 a round Arterial: lose 3 Blood per round; tourniquet or pressure now
Blood left Effect
75% or less Pale and weak: -10% to all actions
50% or less Faint check each minute; -20% to all actions
25% or less Barely conscious: -40% to all actions, can only crawl
None Unconscious and dying

Pain. −10% to attack and defence for each step, counted to 3 steps. Above that, a stop check every round.

Impairments. Each counts once. Attack and defence penalties are capped at −60%.

Leg Movement halved; -20% to footwork and dodging — −20%
Move Movement halved — −10%

Arm (shield arm) That arm -20%; no two-handed use — −10%
Grip (weapon arm) Drops anything held in that hand; cannot grip with it −30% —
Grip (shield arm) Drops anything held in that hand; cannot grip with it — —

The clock. How long the wound takes to kill if left untreated: days, hours, minutes, rounds or instant.

A man with an arm hurt can't use a two-handed weapon: a musket, or a musket with the bayonet. He can only defend until he takes up something else.

First aid. A friend beside him may treat a wound on his turn. Roll d100 against the side's best Leechcraft:

  • Bind: one step less bleeding, 2 steps on a success.
  • Tourniquet: an arm or leg only. The bleeding stops. Left on for hours, the limb is lost.
  • Cauterise: the bleeding stops, at one more step of pain. A success adds no pain.

Armour. Each kit below gives steps off the severity, Critical to Serious to Light to Stopped. A stopped blow is only a bruise. Where a place is only partly covered, read the units digit of the attack roll, with 0 as 10. At or under the cover shown in tens, the blow met the armour.

Part (steps: cut/pierce/crush)Coat (no armour)

No one here wears armour: the French and the British alike fight in their coats.

Range. A musket reaches 25, 50, 100 hexes: short, medium and long. Each hex is 2 yards. On paper take −20 at medium range and −40 at long; the roller does it for you. At night every shot is at −20 more, except at a man in the light of the burning hay (the lit hexes on the map, round each fire). Over the wall no one sees: from the ditch or a ladder a man can shoot only at a man on the parapet (its row of hexes) or on a ladder, and from the rampart a man can shoot into the ditch only from the parapet. A man on the parapet is behind it: −50 to a shot at him from below, unless the hex of the wall's face between him and the shooter is a ladder.

The camp

After the fight, each day runs the same way. Use the camp log.

  1. Evening council. The four roles decide, in this order. A role with nothing to decide is skipped.
    • Leader: stay, move, and what kind of camp.
    • Scout: where to go, and how the watch is set.
    • Quartermaster: what the men eat, and what they try to find.
    • Leech: who gets the medical stores, and how clean the camp is kept.
  2. The day's weather is on the GM's page, and it can make a night hard.
  3. The night. A man in camp gets back 4 Blood.
  4. Wound fever. On the 3rd to 5th day after the fight, roll once for each wound: 5% for low risk, 15% medium, 30% high. Add 5 with no camp, take off 5 in quarters, and take off a leech's Leechcraft ÷ 10. A septic wound moves a step worse, and is checked every night.

Every 7 days: the recovery check. Each wound rolls d100 against the man's Endurance, plus:

What To the roll
Care: no camp -20
Care: a camp +0
Care: quarters in houses +10
He marched that day -20
He rested +10
A night harder than the shelter (cold, wet) -10
Poor hygiene -10
A leech with the force + his Leechcraft ÷ 10
Battle wounds heal easily +20
Wound fever is hard −25

Succeed by 30 or more: two steps better. Succeed: one step better. Fail: it holds, and at deadly he dies. Fail by 30 or more: one step worse. A wound starts on the track at its severity: light is mending, serious is serious, critical is grave. A wound that would kill in days starts at serious at least, and one that would kill in hours or less at grave.

Step In a fight
Healed —
Mending −10% to attack and defence
Serious −25% to attack and defence, cannot run
Grave −25% to attack and defence, crawls only, defends only
Deadly too ill to fight

Every 7 days: sickness. Each well man rolls d100. At or under the chance, he has the flux. A day or so later, roll d100 for how bad: 1–3 deadly, 4–15 grave, otherwise serious.

CampFlux this week, Endurance 50
Quarters, dead buried or far off0%
Watched camp1.5%
Bivouac12.5%
Quarters, dead unburied nearby4%
Watched camp, dead unburied6.5%
Bivouac, dead unburied17.5%

Food. A man carries 4 days' rations. With none left he goes hungry, so forage, buy or move while you can. Hunting in open country or woods: the Quartermaster rolls Fieldcraft at nightfall. A deer feeds 5 men for a day.

Camps. A bivouac needs nothing, and is poor hygiene. A watched camp needs nothing. Quarters in houses need the quartermaster to roll Persuade, and he must find somewhere that will take them.

The escalade

For the GM.

Where and when. Badajoz, on the Spanish frontier with Portugal, the night of 6 to 7 April 1812. Wellington's army has three breaches in the walls, and at ten at night it storms them: about forty attacks are made on the breaches, and all fail (historyofwar). Two escalades away from them succeed. Picton's 3rd Division climbs into the castle, and Leith's 5th Division, late because its ladder party was lost, climbs the bastion of San Vicente. The wall there was "thirty feet high, and the ladders were too short", so the men found a low point and got in by three ladders (Napier, retold; Stanhope has the same height). The division beat off a counter-attack, then went along the walls towards the breaches, and the French there gave way (historyofwar; Kincaid). The 5th lost about 600 men. That much is history. Our four men, this stretch of the rampart and the French on it are ours.

Read this out. The breaches across the town are a roar of musketry and fire. Here it is darker. The ladder is up against the wall, short, its top a man's height under the parapet. A man ahead of you goes up and is gone over the top. Someone above is shouting in French. You climb.

The French. Three men of the garrison hold this stretch of the rampart, a sergent and two fusiliers. Most of the garrison is at the breaches, and these few were not expecting anyone here.

ManWeaponArmourAttackDefenceNerveBlood
FusilierSmoothbore musketUnarmoured50355020
FusilierSmoothbore musketUnarmoured50355020
SergentSmoothbore musketUnarmoured60456520

How it runs.

  1. Set-up (10 minutes). Hand out the sheets and pick the setting. The four start in the ditch at the foot of the ladders. The GM places the French anywhere on the rampart's walk, at least 3 hexes from the parapet, and lights the two fires of burning hay.
  2. Up the ladders. A man at the foot of a ladder climbs on his turn (the ladders, on the quick reference) and comes out on the parapet hex above it on his next turn. The French may shoot down at a man on a ladder, or meet him at the top.
  3. The fight (45 to 60 minutes). Keep a note of the time.
  4. The end. The French nerve check decides it (The fight). A man who surrenders is a prisoner, and the Leader decides what happens to him. If the four lose, the game goes on: they are thrown back into the ditch, and the next company up the ladders takes the rampart an hour later.

After the fight (10 minutes). Bind what can be bound. Then the town opens below them.

The week after

For the GM.

The news. By two in the morning the storm of the breaches is called off, and the French there give way when the 5th Division comes along the walls. The governor surrenders at seven, across the river. The army has lost about 4,670 men killed and wounded in the night. Then the town is sacked: for most of three days the army is out of hand, and it is the people of Badajoz, Spaniards, not the French, who suffer for it. Officers who try to stop it are shot at by their own men. Wellington has a gallows put up, and order comes back slowly (historyofwar; Wikipedia, citing Fletcher and Oman).

The decision that costs something. What do the four do in the sack? Play it as a choice and its cost, not as a scene: the sack happened, and this table needn't linger on it.

Choice What it means
Keep together, and keep out of it They stay on the rampart or with their officers. No plunder. The Leader rolls Command; on a failure one of the four slips away into the town and comes back with something, and trouble.
Guard a house They put themselves between the soldiers and one family. Roll the Leader's Persuade or Command each day of the sack; on a failure there is a fight with their own side's men (the roller's rules, unarmed or with the butt). The family may be worth more to them later than anything they could take.
Go into the town Plunder: each man rolls d100 once on Finds below, and the Quartermaster may sell what they take. Each man also rolls a stop check against his own Nerve at the end of the sack: on a failure he is drunk or in a fight, and starts the next day at −1 Blood. The provosts and the gallows are waiting.
d100 He finds Worth (Days)
1–35 nothing worth the carrying —
36–60 food, tobacco, a blanket 1–3
61–80 boots, a good coat, a knife 3–8
81–92 a purse or a watch 10–30
93–99 silver, a fine weapon 30–90
100 a windfall: jewels, a paymaster's chest 200–1000

Events. Use one on a slow day, or roll d6. Each should make someone decide something.

d6 Event
1 The surgeons' tents by the breaches are full. A wounded man of another company begs the Leech for help before his own.
2 A Spanish woman finds the four: her husband was killed in the sack. She wants them to name the man who did it.
3 The provosts are hanging no one, but they are flogging. One of the four is named by an officer who saw him in the town.
4 Forage: the Quartermaster rolls Persuade or Fieldcraft. On a success, 2 days' rations.
5 Burial parties for the breaches: the dead lie close, and the Leader is asked for men. The dead lie unburied for 14 days unless they go.
6 The army is to march north. A man too weak to march must be left in Badajoz, among the people the army has sacked.

The end of the week. Make the recovery checks and the sickness rolls, then the feedback. Who is alive, and who can march?

If you're using the roller only for the fight, that's fine. Keep the week on paper.

Quick reference

Cut out or print one for each player.

The round. 6 seconds. Initiative d10 + Agility ÷ 10, rolled once; highest first. Every fighter takes one turn.

The one roll. d100 at or under the number. Margin = number − roll. Critical = at or under a tenth of the number.

On his turn. Move: stay, advance 4 and attack, or run 12 and not attack. Leaving an enemy's side gives him a free attack. Attack: d100 against Attack. Aim at a zone or a gap: 20 off the margin each, free on a critical. Defence: d100 against Defence turns it; not against a critical.

How bad. Margin under 20: light. 20+: serious. 50+ or a critical: critical. Margin 2 or less: a graze (a step less bleed and pain, no stop check), unless a critical.

Where and what. d100 on Where it lands under the weapon; cut or thrust is the attacker's choice before rolling (a ball is a shot); a musket shoots every third round, a pistol every fifth. Armour takes steps off: Critical → Serious → Light → Stopped. Part-covered: the attack roll's units digit (0 = 10) at or under the cover's tens met the armour. Read the wound on What it does.

Stop check (S). d100 against Nerve, less pain and blood penalties, 10 more for a critical. Fail: he stops.

Range (musket). Short to 25 hexes, medium to 50 (−20), long to 100 (−40). At night −20 more, unless the target is lit. No one sees over the parapet; a man on it has −50 cover from the ditch.

End of the round. Everyone bleeds: B1, 1 Blood every 10 rounds; B2, 1 a round; B3, 3 a round. A side with 25% or more down, or its leader just down, rolls d100 against its best Nerve still up: +10 with a leader up, −20 if he's down, −20 once 50% are down. Over: the side breaks.

Pain. −10% a step, to 3 steps; above that, a stop check every round. Impairments cap at −60%.

First aid (a friend beside him, his turn, d100 against the side's best Leechcraft). Bind: a step less bleeding, 2 on a success. Tourniquet: arm or leg, bleeding stops. Cauterise: bleeding stops, +1 pain, none on a success.

Lethality. Standard: Blood ×1.5, +20 Nerve on stop checks, 1 fate. Gritty: Blood ×1, no bonus, no fate.

The ladders. Climbing takes a whole turn. A man at the top of a ladder fights at −20, and can't be helped by a friend. A man on a ladder who fails a stop check falls into the ditch: he is out of the fight for 2 rounds, and rolls a stop check again when he lands.
